kurals.tamil:
பேதைமை என்பதொன்று யாதெனின் ஏதங்கொண்டு
ஊதியம் போக விடல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Pedhaimai enbadhondru yaadhenin edhangkondu
oodhiyam poga vidal.
kurals.meaning: If you ask what folly is, it is this: grabbing hold of what harms you and letting what would profit you slip away.
kurals.elementary: Imagine someone offers you a choice between a shiny toy that will break in a day and a bicycle you could ride for years, and you pick the toy and walk away from the bike. That swap, keeping the bad thing and dropping the good one, is exactly what the poet calls being foolish.
kurals.university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a definition rather than an example: pedhaimai (பேதைமை) is the act of taking up edham (ஏதம், harm, loss) and letting oodhiyam (ஊதியம், gain, profit) go. Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar read the pair as a ledger of consequences: the fool does not merely fail to gain, he actively trades gain for loss, which is why folly is placed in the Natpiyal section right after the chapters on bad friendship. Puliyur Kesigan sharpens this into a cost-benefit reading (accepting the trouble that comes with a task while throwing away the profit it would bring), whereas Sivayogi Sivakumar reads edhangkondu as ‘out of fear of a small hardship’, a softer psychological gloss. Kalaignar stresses the failure of discernment: the fool never clarifies which is harmful and which is beneficial. The text is identical in ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Katha Upanishad, Yama tells Nachiketas that the good (shreyas) and the pleasant (preyas) both approach a person; the wise examine and choose the good, while the dull-witted choose the pleasant for the sake of getting and keeping.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad frames life’s basic test as a choice between what truly benefits and what merely attracts, and calls the person who picks wrongly a fool.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar defines folly the same way: choosing what harms over what profits.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close in structure (a fool’s wrong choice between two goods), paraphrased rather than quoted.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright.”
christianity.explanation: The letter to the Hebrews holds up Esau as a warning: a man who traded something of lasting worth for a moment’s appetite.
christianity.tie_back: Esau is the textbook case of taking the small harm and letting the great gain go.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong illustrative match; Hebrews frames it as profanity rather than folly.

islam.quote_or_event: “Those are the ones who have purchased error [in exchange] for guidance, so their transaction has brought no profit, nor were they guided.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes the self-deceived as bad traders who swap guidance for error and walk away with no profit.
islam.tie_back: Both texts use the language of profit and loss to define the fool’s bargain.
islam._accuracy_note: Remarkably close commercial metaphor of losing profit through a bad exchange.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Then Jacob gave Esau bread and pottage of lentiles; and he did eat and drink, and rose up, and went his way: thus Esau despised his birthright.”
judaism.explanation: Genesis tells how Esau, hungry from the field, sold his birthright for a bowl of stew and walked off unconcerned.
judaism.tie_back: The story dramatizes the Kural’s definition: grabbing a passing want and letting a lasting good go.
judaism._accuracy_note: Narrative example rather than a stated principle, but a precise fit.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If by renouncing a lesser happiness one may realize a greater happiness, let the wise man renounce the lesser, having regard for the greater.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada advises giving up a small pleasure when doing so secures a larger one.
buddhism.tie_back: It is the wise mirror image of the fool in the Kural, who gives up the greater gain for the lesser.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Inverse statement of the same principle.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod tells how Epimetheus, though warned by Prometheus never to accept a gift from Zeus, took in Pandora and understood the harm only after it was already his.
greek_mythology.explanation: Epimetheus, whose name means ‘afterthought’, accepts the gift that carries every evil into the world.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like Valluvar’s fool, he takes in the harm and loses the good he had been warned to keep.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good narrative fit; paraphrased, and the myth stresses heedlessness more than a gain-loss trade.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Protagoras, Socrates argues that people choose worse over better because they mismeasure pleasures and pains, and that the remedy is an art of measurement; the failure he calls ignorance.
philosophy.explanation: For Socrates, choosing the larger harm for the smaller benefit is a failure of knowledge, not of desire.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar likewise defines folly as a mistaken weighing of harm against gain.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Conceptually close; Plato’s argument is broader and more technical.

kurals.tamil:
பேதைமையுள் எல்லாம் பேதைமை காதன்மை
கையல்ல தன்கட் செயல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Pedhaimaiyul ellaam pedhaimai kaadhanmai
kaiyalla thankat seyal.
kurals.meaning: The worst folly of all is to set one’s heart on deeds that are not fitting for oneself.
kurals.elementary: A goldfish might dream of climbing trees like a squirrel, but if it jumps out of its bowl to try, it will only get hurt. The silliest mistake is wanting badly to do things that are not right for who you are.
kurals.university: The couplet ranks follies and puts at the top kaadhanmai (காதன்மை, fond desire, love) for kaiyalla (கையல்ல, what is not within one’s proper hand or conduct). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar take kaiyalla as acts unsuited to one’s own moral conduct (ஒழுக்கம்), which matches G. U. Pope’s ‘deeds which to your station unbefitting prove’ and Drew’s ‘delight in doing what is forbidden’. Kalaignar instead reads it as deeds beyond one’s ability, Solomon Pappaiah as desiring things that do one no good, and Puliyur Kesigan as both choosing an undesirable act and doing it unfittingly; the line thus spans a moral reading (forbidden) and a prudential one (beyond one’s scope). The wording is the same in ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is far better to discharge one’s prescribed duties, even though faultily, than another’s duties perfectly. Destruction in the course of performing one’s own duty is better than engaging in another’s duties, for to follow another’s path is dangerous.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns Arjuna against taking up a role that is not his own, however attractive it seems.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural similarly calls it the height of folly to love deeds that do not belong to one’s own path.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close on ‘what is not one’s own’; the Gita frames it as svadharma rather than folly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed. Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death.”
christianity.explanation: James traces wrongdoing back to a desire that pulls a person toward what he should not do.
christianity.tie_back: Valluvar likewise locates the worst folly in desire (kaadhanmai) fixed on unfitting deeds.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the focus on misdirected desire; James speaks of sin, not folly.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not walk upon the earth exultantly. Indeed, you will never tear the earth [apart], and you will never reach the mountains in height.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an rebukes the person who strides about as though he could do what is far beyond his measure.
islam.tie_back: Both warn against reaching for what lies outside one’s rightful scope.
islam._accuracy_note: Partial match: about arrogance and overreach rather than desire for unfitting deeds.

judaism.quote_or_event: “LORD, my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty: neither do I exercise myself in great matters, or in things too high for me.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist claims a quiet humility that does not grasp at matters beyond his reach.
judaism.tie_back: It describes the wise opposite of the Kural’s fool, who sets his heart on what does not befit him.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good fit for the ‘beyond one’s station’ reading; not phrased as a warning about folly.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The fool seeks undeserved reputation, precedence among monks, authority over monasteries, and honor among householders.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada’s chapter on the fool describes him as hungry for positions and honours that do not fit him.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar’s fool, too, sets his heart on what is not properly his.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close: both name the fool’s desire for what is unbecoming to him.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Bellerophon, after his victories, tried to ride the winged horse Pegasus up to the dwelling of the gods and was thrown back down to earth.
greek_mythology.explanation: Pindar uses the story to warn that reaching for what belongs to the gods ends in a fall.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It pictures the Kural’s chief folly: desiring a deed that is not one’s own to do.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong image of unfitting ambition; the myth is about hubris more than folly.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Republic, Socrates defines justice as each person doing his own work and not meddling in what belongs to another.
philosophy.explanation: Plato treats staying within one’s proper task as the basis of a well-ordered soul and city.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar likewise counts it the worst folly to love deeds that are not one’s own.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Parallel principle; Plato speaks of justice rather than folly.

kurals.tamil:
நாணாமை நாடாமை நாரின்மை யாதொன்றும்
பேணாமை பேதை தொழில்.
kurals.transliteration:
Naanaamai naadaamai naarinmai yaadhondrum
penaamai pedhai thozhil.
kurals.meaning: Feeling no shame at wrong, not seeking what is worth seeking, having no affection, and caring for nothing at all: these are the habits of the fool.
kurals.elementary: Think of a kid who breaks a window and doesn’t feel sorry, never tries to learn anything, isn’t kind to friends, and leaves their toys out in the rain. Each of those things on its own is a warning sign; together they are what the poet calls a fool.
kurals.university: The couplet is a fourfold catalogue built on negative nouns ending in -aamai/-inmai: naanaamai (நாணாமை, shamelessness at what deserves shame), naadaamai (நாடாமை, not seeking out what deserves seeking), naarinmai (நாரின்மை, lack of naar, ‘fibre’, a metaphor for the affection that binds people), and penaamai (பேணாமை, not cherishing or protecting anything). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar gloss naar as anbu (love), and the commentators agree the list describes a whole disposition rather than isolated faults; Pope renders it ‘Ashamed of nothing, searching nothing out, of loveless heart, / Nought cherishing’. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads naarinmai as lacking sweetness of manner, a minor variation. The text is identical in both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Those who are demoniac do not know what is to be done and what is not to be done. Neither cleanliness nor proper behavior nor truth is found in them.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita’s portrait of the demoniac nature is a list of absences: no sense of right action, no purity, no truth.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar likewise defines the fool by what is missing in him: shame, seeking, love and care.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Similar catalogue of lacks, though the items listed differ.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes people who boast of what ought to embarrass them and care only for appetite.
christianity.tie_back: It matches the Kural’s first mark of the fool, shamelessness at what deserves shame.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the shamelessness element only, not the full fourfold list.

islam.quote_or_event: “One of the sayings of the early Prophets which the people have got is: If you don't feel ashamed … do whatever you like.”
islam.explanation: The hadith treats haya’ (a sense of shame) as the brake on bad conduct: once it is gone, anything goes.
islam.tie_back: Valluvar puts naanaamai, absence of shame, first among the fool’s traits for the same reason.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 6120 (sunnah.com; translator’s parenthetical gloss elided)
islam._accuracy_note: Direct parallel on shamelessness; covers one of the four traits.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Were they ashamed when they had committed abomination? nay, they were not at all ashamed, neither could they blush: therefore they shall fall among them that fall.”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah condemns a people who have lost the ability to blush at their own wrongdoing.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts see the loss of shame as a sign of ruin.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on shamelessness; does not address the other three traits.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Those who are ashamed of what they should not be ashamed of, and are not ashamed of what they should be ashamed of — upholding false views, they go to states of woe.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says misplaced shame, especially no shame where it is due, leads to suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar’s naanaamai is exactly shamelessness at what should shame us.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Precise on the shame element; the other traits are absent.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod foresees a degenerate age in which Aidos (Shame) and Nemesis (Righteous Indignation) wrap themselves in white robes and leave the earth, abandoning humankind to grief.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth shame is a goddess, and her departure marks the moral collapse of a whole generation.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural likewise treats the absence of shame as the root mark of the fool.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Thematic link on shame only; concerns a whole age, not an individual fool.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle says shame (aidos) befits the young, who live by feeling and make mistakes, because it holds them back; and he calls the person who would feel no shame at disgraceful acts base.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle treats a sense of shame as a safeguard for those not yet fully virtuous.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s fool lacks exactly this safeguard.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; parallels the shamelessness trait only.

kurals.tamil:
ஓதி உணர்ந்தும் பிறர்க்குரைத்தும் தானடங்காப்
பேதையின் பேதையார் இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Odhi unarndhum pirarkkuraiththum thaanadangaap
pedhaiyin pedhaiyaar il.
kurals.meaning: No fool is greater than the one who has studied, understood, and even taught others, yet does not himself live by what he learned.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a swimming coach who teaches everyone how to stay safe in the pool but then jumps into the deep end without looking. Knowing the rules and telling others is not enough; the biggest silliness is not following them yourself.
kurals.university: The couplet climbs three steps, odhi (ஓதி, having recited or studied), unarndhum (உணர்ந்தும், having understood) and pirarkku uraiththum (பிறர்க்கு உரைத்தும், having explained to others), and then collapses on thaan adangaa (தான் அடங்கா, himself not restrained, not conforming). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar take adangudhal as living within the discipline the texts teach, and the superlative pedhaiyin pedhaiyaar il (‘there is no fool beyond this fool’) makes the learned hypocrite the extreme case of the chapter. Puliyur Kesigan glosses adangaa as lacking self-restraint (adakkam), linking the couplet to the chapter on Adakkamudaimai. All four commentaries and the two base texts agree on the reading.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A well-known verse of the Hitopadesha says that people remain fools even after studying the scriptures, and that the one who acts on them is the truly learned person.
hinduism.explanation: The Sanskrit fable collection holds that learning proves itself only in practice.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar makes the same point: knowing and teaching without living it is the deepest folly.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close in meaning; paraphrased and verse number not verified against a live edition.

christianity.quote_or_event: “All therefore whatsoever they bid you observe, that observe and do; but do not ye after their works: for they say, and do not.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells the crowds to follow what the teachers of the law teach but not to copy their conduct, because they do not practise it.
christianity.tie_back: ‘They say, and do not’ is Valluvar’s learned fool in four words.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on teaching without practising.

islam.quote_or_event: “Do you order righteousness of the people and forget yourselves while you recite the Scripture? Then will you not reason?”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an rebukes those who preach goodness and recite scripture but neglect it in their own lives, and calls this a failure of reason.
islam.tie_back: Both texts name reciting, preaching, and not practising as the height of unreason.
islam._accuracy_note: Almost exact parallel, including the link to lack of reason.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Study is not the most important thing, but actions.”
judaism.explanation: Shimon son of Rabban Gamaliel teaches that learning finds its purpose in deeds.
judaism.tie_back: Valluvar likewise judges study worthless, even foolish, without conduct to match.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close principle; Avot does not use the language of folly.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Much though he recites the sacred texts, but acts not accordingly, that heedless man is like a cowherd who only counts the cows of others — he does not partake of the blessings of the holy life.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares the learned non-practitioner to a hired herdsman counting cattle that are not his.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts say that reciting without practising gains a person nothing.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Plato recounts the story of Thales, who fell into a well while gazing at the stars, and a Thracian servant girl joked that he was eager to know the heavens but could not see what lay at his feet.
greek_mythology.explanation: The anecdote mocks learning that never reaches one’s own steps.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like Valluvar’s fool, the scholar knows much but fails in his own conduct.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A philosophical anecdote rather than myth, and about impracticality rather than moral hypocrisy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus advises never to call yourself a philosopher or talk about principles among ordinary people, but to act on them, just as sheep show how much they have eaten not by bringing up grass but by producing wool and milk.
philosophy.explanation: For Epictetus, philosophy is proven by conduct, not by lecturing.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar equally scorns the one who teaches but does not live the teaching.

kurals.tamil:
ஒருமைச் செயலாற்றும் பேதை எழுமையும்
தான்புக் கழுந்தும் அளறு.
kurals.transliteration:
Orumaich cheyalaatrum pedhai ezhumaiyum
thaanpuk kazhundhum alaru.
kurals.meaning: In a single lifetime the fool can bring about the hell into which he will sink through all seven births to come.
kurals.elementary: A few minutes of scribbling with permanent marker on your bedroom wall can leave a mess that takes weeks to clean. The poet says the foolish person can make, in one life, a mess so big it sticks to him for a very long time.
kurals.university: The couplet sets orumai (ஒருமை, one birth) against ezhumai (எழுமை, the seven births), and alaru (அளறு, literally ‘mire’ or ‘mud’) is the traditional word for naragam, hell. Parimelazhagar, Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah all read it eschatologically: in one life the fool is able to make (ஆற்றும்) the hell he will enter and sink into across seven births. Kalaignar departs from this, reading orumaich cheyal as ‘self-willed action’ and alaru as a mire of suffering in this world, a deliberately non-theological gloss; Puliyur Kesigan’s note on thirukkural.net is truncated. Pope’s ‘The fool will merit hell in one brief life on earth’ follows the traditional reading. The text is the same in both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Those who are envious and mischievous, who are the lowest among men, I perpetually cast into the ocean of material existence, into various demoniac species of life.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes how persistent wrong conduct leads to repeated low births within samsara.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar’s fool likewise builds, in one life, a hell that follows him through many births.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Same rebirth framework; the Gita speaks of the envious and cruel rather than fools.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap. For he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting.”
christianity.explanation: Paul teaches that what a person sows in this life decides what he reaps, even into eternity.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural similarly says the fool’s one life sows a harvest of long suffering.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the consequence principle; no rebirth framework.

islam.quote_or_event: “And they will say, ‘If only we had been listening or reasoning, we would not be among the companions of the Blaze.’”
islam.explanation: The people of the Fire confess that their failure to listen and to reason in this life is what put them there.
islam.tie_back: Both texts tie unreason in one life to lasting punishment after it.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close: folly in this life explicitly causes the hereafter’s fire.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs warns that a path chosen without wisdom can lead to ruin even when it looks right.
judaism.tie_back: Valluvar’s fool likewise walks confidently into a lasting downfall.
judaism._accuracy_note: Shares the theme of self-made ruin, without the many-births idea.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Fools of little wit are enemies unto themselves as they move about doing evil deeds, the fruits of which are bitter.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says the fool is his own worst enemy, planting deeds whose fruit is bitter.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar’s fool, too, digs his own hell by his own actions.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close on the self-made suffering of the fool.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the underworld Odysseus sees Tityos, Tantalus and Sisyphus undergoing endless punishments for wrongs committed in their lifetimes.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer pictures the afterlife as the place where one life’s misdeeds become unending suffering.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural similarly makes one lifetime’s folly the cause of long-lasting torment.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Shares eternal consequence; the sinners are proud offenders, not fools.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Myth of Er, the soul that drew the first lot hastily chose the life of a great tyrant without examining it, and only afterwards discovered it was fated to devour its own children; Plato notes he had lived his previous life in a well-ordered city by habit, without philosophy.
philosophy.explanation: Plato shows how an unexamined choice can doom a soul across its next life.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s fool likewise sets the course of many births by one life’s foolish deeds.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; good fit on folly shaping future lives.

kurals.tamil:
பொய்படும் ஒன்றோ புனைபூணும் கையறியாப்
பேதை வினைமேற் கொளின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Poipadum ondro punaipoonum kaiyariyaap
pedhai vinaimer kolin.
kurals.meaning: When a fool who does not know how to do a thing takes on a task, the work fails, and not only that: he ends up putting himself in chains.
kurals.elementary: If someone who has never cooked tries to make a big dinner alone, the food gets burnt, and they might also burn their hand. Taking on a job you don’t know how to do can spoil the job and hurt you too.
kurals.university: Kaiyariyaa (கையறியா) means ‘not knowing the method’ (kai here is the way of doing), and the couplet’s rhetorical ondro (ஒன்றோ, ‘is it only one thing?’) introduces a double penalty: the work poipadum (பொய்படும், comes to nothing) and the doer punai poonum (புனைபூணும், wears fetters). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesigan take punai literally as the shackles of a man held culpable, which Pope follows (‘himself he binds with chains’), while Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar soften it to ‘he too is ruined’ or ‘punishes himself’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss kaiyariyaa morally (not knowing the right way of conduct), whereas Pappaiah reads it practically (not knowing how to do the work). Both base sources give the same text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That action performed in illusion, in disregard of scriptural injunctions, and without concern for future bondage or for violence or distress caused to others is said to be in the mode of ignorance.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita classes as tamasic any work begun in delusion without weighing its consequences, including future bondage.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar’s ignorant undertaker likewise ruins the work and binds himself.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good fit, including the striking ‘future bondage’ parallel to fetters.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it? Lest haply, after he hath laid the foundation, and is not able to finish it, all that behold it begin to mock him, Saying, This man began to build, and was not able to finish.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that starting a project without weighing one’s ability leads to failure and public shame.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts describe a task begun without competence that ends in failure and harm to the doer.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close on failed undertaking; the penalty is mockery rather than fetters.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight and the heart - about all those [one] will be questioned.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids acting on what one does not know and warns that one will be held accountable.
islam.tie_back: Valluvar’s fool takes up work he does not understand and pays for it.
islam._accuracy_note: Shares the principle of not acting without knowledge, plus accountability.

judaism.quote_or_event: “His own iniquities shall take the wicked himself, and he shall be holden with the cords of his sins. He shall die without instruction; and in the greatness of his folly he shall go astray.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs pictures the wrongdoer caught and bound by the cords of his own actions, led astray by folly.
judaism.tie_back: The image of being bound by one’s own folly mirrors the Kural’s self-imposed fetters.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong binding image; concerns wickedness more than incompetence.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Aramadusaka Jataka, monkeys left to water a king’s garden pull up every sapling to check the length of its roots so they can measure the water, and the whole garden withers.
buddhism.explanation: The Bodhisatta remarks that fools, trying to do good, end up doing harm.
buddhism.tie_back: It is a vivid picture of the Kural’s fool who takes on work he does not understand and ruins it.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good fit on botched work; lacks the self-inflicted fetters.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Phaethon begged to drive the chariot of the Sun for one day, could not control the horses, set the earth on fire, and was struck down by Zeus’s thunderbolt.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid tells it as the tale of a youth who took on a task far beyond his skill.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, the work is ruined and the doer is destroyed with it.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very close: ignorant undertaking, failed task and self-ruin.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Apology, Socrates reports that the craftsmen he questioned truly knew their crafts, but because of that skill thought themselves wise in other weighty matters too, and this error overshadowed their wisdom.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates exposes people who act as experts beyond the reach of their real knowledge.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s fool likewise takes on work whose method he does not know.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Shares overreach beyond competence; no ruined task or self-binding.

kurals.tamil:
ஏதிலார் ஆரத் தமர்பசிப்பர் பேதை
பெருஞ்செல்வம் உற்றக் கடை.
kurals.transliteration:
Edhilaar aarath thamarpasippar pedhai
perunjelvam utrak kadai.
kurals.meaning: When a fool comes into great wealth, strangers feast on it while his own people go hungry.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a boy who wins a huge bag of candy and hands it all out to kids he barely knows, while his little sister at home gets none. Having lots of something doesn’t help your family if you don’t know how to share it wisely.
kurals.university: The couplet contrasts edhilaar (ஏதிலார், strangers, those with no tie) who aara (ஆர, eat their fill) with thamar (தமர், one’s own kin) who pasippar (பசிப்பர், go hungry). Puliyur Kesigan follows the traditional explanation that the fool’s wealth comes from past merit (munvinai), while the lack of judgment in spending it is his own; Parimelazhagar’s tradition reads the strangers as flatterers and parasites who gather round new wealth. Kalaignar’s gloss stresses that outsiders ‘roll up’ the money while affectionate kin go without. Pope renders edhilaar as ‘foes’, a stronger word than the Tamil requires; Drew’s ‘neighbours’ is closer. The text is the same in both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And charity performed at an impure place, at an improper time, to unworthy persons, or without proper attention and respect is said to be in the mode of ignorance.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita classes giving to the wrong people, at the wrong time and place, as charity in ignorance.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar’s fool likewise lavishes his wealth on the wrong people while his own go short.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Parallel on misdirected giving; does not mention neglected kin.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says that neglecting one’s own household is a basic moral failure.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s fool commits exactly this failure, feeding strangers and starving kin.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on the neglected-kin side; says nothing of strangers profiting.

islam.quote_or_event: “And give the relative his right, and [also] the poor and the traveler, and do not spend wastefully.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an puts relatives first among those with a claim on one’s wealth and forbids squandering it.
islam.tie_back: Valluvar’s fool reverses this order, wasting wealth on outsiders while kin go hungry.
islam._accuracy_note: Good fit on kin’s right and wasteful spending.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A man to whom God hath given riches, wealth, and honour, so that he wanteth nothing for his soul of all that he desireth, yet God giveth him not power to eat thereof, but a stranger eateth it: this is vanity, and it is an evil disease.”
judaism.explanation: Ecclesiastes laments the man whose great wealth ends up feeding a stranger rather than himself.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts picture abundant wealth consumed by strangers instead of those it should serve.
judaism._accuracy_note: Striking image match, though Ecclesiastes blames fate rather than folly.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sigalovada Sutta, the Buddha warns young Sigala of the channels through which wealth is squandered, such as drink, gambling and bad companions, and teaches that one should support friends and relatives with gifts and kindly care.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta pairs wise use of wealth with duties to one’s own circle.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar’s fool fails at both: his wealth leaks to outsiders and his kin go hungry.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; parallel advice rather than the same image.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Odysseus’s absence, the suitors occupy his house and feast day after day on his herds and wine, while Penelope and Telemachus look on helplessly.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer makes the wasting of a household’s wealth by outsiders a central wrong of the Odyssey.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It mirrors the Kural’s picture of strangers feasting while the family suffers.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong image match, but the cause is the owner’s absence, not his folly.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle says the prodigal gives to the wrong people, enriching flatterers and others who deserve nothing, while failing to give to those who should receive.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, prodigality is a failure to give to the right people in the right amounts.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s fool shows exactly this vice: outsiders grow fat while kin go hungry.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close analysis of misdirected giving, paraphrased.

kurals.tamil:
மையல் ஒருவன் களித்தற்றால் பேதைதன்
கையொன்று உடைமை பெறின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Maiyal oruvan kaliththatraal pedhaidhan
kaiyondru udaimai perin.
kurals.meaning: When a fool gets something into his hands, it is like a man already out of his mind who has also become drunk.
kurals.elementary: Picture a kid who is already running wild at a party and then gets a big bag of sugar. Things go from silly to much worse! Giving power or money to someone who doesn’t think clearly only makes their foolishness bigger.
kurals.university: The simile doubles the condition: maiyal (மையல், bewilderment, madness) is a man already deranged, and kaliththal (களித்தல்) is intoxication by toddy, so the fool who gains udaimai (உடைமை, possession) is a madman who is also drunk. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both gloss maiyal as piththu (பித்து, madness) and kaliththal as being dazed by kal (கள், toddy), and Puliyur Kesigan adds that such a man drinks more and more and strays from his course. Kai ondru (கை ஒன்று) is read as ‘anything in his hand’, so the point holds for any wealth or authority, not only great fortune. Pope (‘as when a mad man raves in drunken glee’) and Drew follow the same reading, and the two base sources agree on the text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The demoniac person thinks: ‘So much wealth do I have today, and I will gain more according to my schemes. So much is mine now, and it will increase in the future, more and more…’ In this way, such persons are deluded by ignorance.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita shows wealth swelling the deluded person’s arrogance into a kind of intoxication.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar likewise says possession makes an already confused mind drunk.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good fit on wealth deepening delusion; excerpted from a longer passage.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And I will say to my soul, Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry. But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the rich fool, abundance makes a man complacent and heedless of what matters.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts show possessions intoxicating the fool rather than steadying him.
christianity._accuracy_note: Explicitly about a ‘fool’ and wealth; stresses complacency more than frenzy.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not give the weak-minded your property, which Allāh has made a means of sustenance for you, but provide for them with it and clothe them and speak to them words of appropriate kindness.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids handing control of property to those who lack sound judgment, while still providing for them.
islam.tie_back: It rests on the same insight as the Kural: wealth in a fool’s hands does harm.
islam._accuracy_note: Direct legal parallel to the danger of the fool holding property.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For three things the earth is disquieted, and for four which it cannot bear: For a servant when he reigneth; and a fool when he is filled with meat;”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs lists a fool who has plenty among the things the world cannot bear.
judaism.tie_back: Valluvar likewise says a fool with possessions becomes worse, like a madman made drunk.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close: a fool made full becomes intolerable.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Riches ruin only the foolish, not those in quest of the Beyond. By craving for riches the witless man ruins himself as well as others.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says wealth is dangerous only in the hands of the foolish.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts say possession magnifies the fool’s folly into ruin.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close match on wealth ruining the fool.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas, granted any wish by Dionysus, foolishly asked that everything he touched turn to gold, and soon found he could not eat or drink.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid shows a foolish man given power turning a gift into a curse.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s fool, Midas is made worse, not better, by what comes into his hands.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good illustration; Midas’s folly is in the wish, not the frenzy after it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle describes the character that wealth produces as insolent and arrogant, as if possessed by their riches, behaving like people who think they have every good thing; he calls this a prosperous fool.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle observes that sudden wealth distorts character, especially in those without judgment.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar says the same: possession intoxicates the foolish.

kurals.tamil:
பெரிதினிது பேதையார் கேண்மை பிரிவின்கண்
பீழை தருவதொன் றில்.
kurals.transliteration:
Peridhinidhu pedhaiyaar kenmai pirivinkan
peezhai tharuvadhon ril.
kurals.meaning: Friendship with fools is very sweet indeed, for when it ends, there is nothing in the parting that causes any pain.
kurals.elementary: Some friends are like a balloon on a string: it is fun for a while, but when it floats away you don’t really miss it. The poet is joking that friends who are foolish are ‘lovely’, because losing them doesn’t hurt at all.
kurals.university: The couplet is ironic praise: peridhu inidhu (பெரிது இனிது, ‘exceedingly sweet’) is applied to pedhaiyaar kenmai (பேதையார் கேண்மை, friendship with fools), and the reason given is that at pirivu (பிரிவு, separation) there is no peezhai (பீழை, pain, affliction). Mu. Varadarasanar, Kalaignar and Puliyur Kesigan all read it as saying that a fool’s friendship is ‘sweet’ only in that losing it costs nothing, so its real worth is zero; Kesigan hedges with ‘in one way’. Solomon Pappaiah reads it slightly differently, as friendship among fools themselves, whose partings cause them no grief, which matches Drew’s ‘the friendship between fools’. The text is the same in ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhartrhari’s Nitishataka says one might pull a jewel from a crocodile’s jaws or wear a raging serpent like a flower, but one cannot win over a fool whose mind is set wrong.
hinduism.explanation: The Sanskrit poet treats the fool as someone no real bond can be formed with.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar’s irony makes a similar point: friendship with a fool has so little in it that losing it costs nothing.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Weak match: about the futility of reaching a fool, not the painless parting; verse number not verified.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners.”
christianity.explanation: Paul, quoting a Greek proverb, warns that bad company damages character.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts imply that friendship with fools is worth little and well lost.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the low value of foolish company but lacks the irony about painless parting.

islam.quote_or_event: “Close friends, that Day, will be enemies to each other, except for the righteous”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says friendships not grounded in righteousness will fall apart on the Day of Judgment.
islam.tie_back: Valluvar likewise implies that friendships without wisdom have nothing in them that lasts.
islam._accuracy_note: Partial: shows such friendships are hollow, not that their loss is painless.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Go from the presence of a foolish man, when thou perceivest not in him the lips of knowledge.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs advises simply leaving the company of a fool once you see he has no wisdom to offer.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s irony points the same way: walking away from a fool costs nothing.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good practical parallel; lacks the ironic tone.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Good is it to see the Noble Ones; to live with them is ever blissful. One will always be happy by not encountering fools.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says plainly that life is happier without fools in it.
buddhism.tie_back: Valluvar’s joke rests on the same truth: separation from a fool brings no grief.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close in substance, stated directly rather than ironically.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable of the travellers and the bear, one companion scrambles up a tree and leaves his friend to face the bear; the bear seems to whisper to the man on the ground never to travel with a friend who deserts at the first sign of danger.
greek_mythology.explanation: The fable shows a friendship that proves worthless the moment it is tested.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like Valluvar’s fool’s friendship, it is one whose loss is no loss.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Fable rather than myth, and about a treacherous friend rather than a foolish one.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle explains that friendships based on pleasure or usefulness are easily dissolved, since when the pleasure or use ends, the friendship ends too.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, only friendship grounded in virtue endures; the rest come apart without much loss.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s fool’s friendship is the shallow kind whose ending leaves no wound.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close analysis of shallow friendship, paraphrased.

kurals.tamil:
கழாஅக்கால் பள்ளியுள் வைத்தற்றால் சான்றோர்
குழாஅத்துப் பேதை புகல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kazhaaakkaal palliyul vaiththatraal saandror
kuzhaaaththup pedhai pugal.
kurals.meaning: A fool entering an assembly of the wise is like putting unwashed feet on a clean bed.
kurals.elementary: Imagine coming in from a muddy football field and climbing straight into a freshly made bed with dirty feet. Everything gets messy. The poet says a fool barging into a group of wise people spoils things in the same way.
kurals.university: The closing simile sets kazhaaak kaal (கழாஅக்கால், unwashed foot) in palli (பள்ளி) against the fool’s pugal (புகல், entering) into saandror kuzhaaam (சான்றோர் குழாஅம், the gathering of the noble). The lengthened forms kazhaaa- and kuzhaaa- are isai-nirai alapedai (இசைநிறை அளபெடை), vowel prolongation that fills out the metre. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar take palli as a bed (as do Pope and Drew), but Puliyur Kesigan reads it as a place of worship (‘தொழுகைக்குரிய பள்ளி’), making the image one of defiling a sanctuary; both senses of palli are attested in Tamil. The text is identical in both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Bhartrhari’s Nitishataka calls silence the cover the Creator gave to hide ignorance, and says it is the ornament of the unlearned above all in an assembly of the learned.
hinduism.explanation: The Sanskrit verse advises the ignorant to keep quiet when among the wise.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar sees the fool’s presence in a learned gathering as a defilement; Bhartrhari offers the fool his only remedy.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Same setting (fool among the learned); verse number not verified against a live edition.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And when the king came in to see the guests, he saw there a man which had not on a wedding garment: And he saith unto him, Friend, how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment? And he was speechless.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the wedding feast, a guest who enters unprepared is challenged and has no answer.
christianity.tie_back: Like the unwashed foot on the bed, he brings into a pure gathering what does not belong there.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good image of unfit entry into a worthy gathering; the parable’s meaning is eschatological.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, when you rise to [perform] prayer, wash your faces and your forearms to the elbows and wipe over your heads and wash your feet to the ankles.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an requires washing, including the feet, before standing in prayer.
islam.tie_back: On Kesigan’s reading of palli as a place of worship, the Kural’s image is the very impurity this washing prevents.
islam._accuracy_note: A ritual rule, not a teaching on fools; the link is the shared image of unwashed feet.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Therefore the ungodly shall not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous.”
judaism.explanation: The first psalm says the wicked have no place in the gathering of the righteous.
judaism.tie_back: Valluvar likewise sees the fool as out of place in the assembly of the wise.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close on not belonging among the worthy; speaks of sinners, not fools.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Though all his life a fool associates with a wise man, he no more comprehends the Truth than a spoon tastes the flavor of the soup.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says a fool can sit among the wise for a lifetime and absorb nothing.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts see the fool in wise company as out of place and unchanged.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Same setting; stresses the fool’s inability to learn rather than his defiling presence.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When the mountain god Tmolus judged the music contest between Apollo and Pan and gave the prize to Apollo, Midas alone objected; Apollo gave him the ears of an ass for his dull hearing.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid shows a fool pushing his opinion into a contest judged by the divine and the wise, and being marked for it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like Valluvar’s fool entering the assembly of the wise, Midas spoils the gathering and disgraces himself.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good narrative fit for a fool among the wise.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Phaedo, Socrates says that it is not permitted for the impure to lay hold of the pure, which is why the soul must be cleansed before it can grasp truth.
philosophy.explanation: Plato treats purification as a precondition for entering into contact with what is pure.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s unwashed foot on a clean bed is a homely image of the same incompatibility.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Shares the pure/impure image; Plato’s context is the soul and knowledge, not social gatherings.
